fatal_errors: The proposed Hf-to-Al substitution does not reconstruct the target intervention of adding 4.2 at.% Cr by vacuum arc melting.

The baseline ductility is incorrectly stated as approximately 50%; the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline has a room-temperature fracture strain of about 11.6%, while the greater-than-50% value belongs to HfNbTaTiZr.
Replacing only 10–20% of the single Hf component is unlikely to reduce total alloy density by the claimed 7–10%; the target density prediction is not supported by a rule-of-mixtures calculation.
The hypothesis omits the target reticulated Cr2(Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta) Laves-phase mediator and instead assumes that intermetallic formation should be avoided.
The cited evidence does not directly establish that Al substitution in HfMoTaTiZr preserves room-temperature ductility or 1000 °C strength.
explanation: The answer addresses the broad density–strength trade-off and proposes a single, testable compositional intervention. Its alloy series, matched control, density measurements, two test temperatures, and quantitative rejection thresholds make it a reasonably discriminating alternative experiment. However, it diverges completely from the target Cr-addition intervention and its reticulated Laves-phase mechanism. Only the generic idea of substitutional lattice-distortion strengthening overlaps mechanistically. Baseline ductility is misassigned from another RHEA, and the predicted density reduction is quantitatively doubtful because Al replaces only a fraction of one of five nominal components. Evidence E2 supports low-density-element alloy design only in general, while E1 concerns a chemically and structurally different AlCoCrFeNi eutectic alloy. Allowing unspecified heat treatments and either tensile or compression loading also weakens control relative to the as-cast, room-temperature compression target.
